screens.title: Advanced Asset Management & Addressables
screens.subtitle: From build-time bloat to runtime control: scale asset loading, memory, and live updates

narration.text: In larger Unity projects, the default way Unity ties assets to scenes quickly becomes a bottleneck. You will learn why loading everything referenced by a scene creates long load times and memory spikes, and how the Addressables system lets you break that tight coupling. Addressables lets you give assets a stable address or label, load them asynchronously, and host them locally or remotely without changing game code. In practical terms this means quicker startup, finer memory control, and the ability to ship new levels or cosmetics as downloadable content. We will walk through installation, how to make assets addressable, how groups and build profiles control packaging and hosting, and crucial memory management patterns such as releasing AsyncOperationHandles. As an example, you will see how simple prefabs and materials can be converted to Addressables, loaded at runtime, and released so the profiler shows memory returning to expected levels. By the end you should be able to plan groups for predictable updates and avoid common leaks. Consider how this approach changes the way your game is built and updated.

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Addressables decouple asset references from scenes, enabling on-demand asynchronous loading, better memory control, and remote updates without rebuilding the client.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll be able to demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: This chapter sets specific, practical goals so you can build an Addressables workflow that scales. First, you will identify the limitations of Unity's traditional loading patterns such as scene references and Resources folders, and explain why those patterns create long load times and build bloat. Second, you will install and initialize the Addressables package, create groups, and assign assets an address or label so they can be managed independently of scenes. Third, you will use the asynchronous Addressables A P I to load assets at runtime and work with AsyncOperationHandle objects. Finally, you will practice the habit that prevents leaks: releasing handles and destroying spawned instances correctly. Each objective is framed around a concrete task, such as migrating prefabs and materials to Addressables and observing memory changes in the Profiler. As you practice these tasks you will move from understanding the problem to applying the Addressables workflow in real projects.

screens.title: Why traditional Unity loading fails at scale
screens.subtitle: Scene references, Resources folders, and manual bundles explained

narration.text: First, understand the core problem: Unity's default asset wiring loads everything a scene references when the scene loads. That is convenient for small projects but devastating for large content sets. If a level references many characters, textures, and audio clips, they all get pulled into memory whether they are needed immediately or not. The Resources folder offers name-based loading, but every asset placed in Resources is baked into the build, causing bloat even if never used at runtime. The manual Asset Bundle approach can avoid some of this, but building and maintaining bundles by hand requires custom dependency tracking and complex loading logic. Addressables solves this by abstracting away manual bundles and replacing tight references with addressable handles. A concrete example: an open-world game that used scene references for all NPC models experienced long load times because dozens of character meshes were loaded at once. A common misconception is thinking that Destroying an instantiated object will always free the backing asset. In reality, if the asset's handle is still retained by the loading system, memory stays allocated. The core takeaway is that you must separate the runtime instance lifetime from the asset reference lifetime and control asset residency; this is where Addressables provides the right primitives.

keyIdea.title: Problem Statement
keyIdea.text: Scene references and Resources lead to build and memory bloat; manual bundles are complex. Addressables provides an abstraction to avoid both pitfalls.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why default loading doesn't scale
Understand the mechanics that cause long load times and build bloat in large projects.
Scene references load every referenced asset at scene load, even transient ones.
Resources includes all assets in the build regardless of runtime usage, causing bloat.
Manual Asset Bundles work but demand custom logic for dependencies and versioning.
Concrete example
An open-world level referenced dozens of NPC prefabs. All meshes and textures were loaded on scene load, causing a long pause. Moving those prefabs to an on-demand workflow reduced startup time.
Key Takeaway

Default references are simple but inflexible. To scale, replace tight references with addressable patterns that support on-demand loading and unloading.

Misconception
Destroying a spawned GameObject does not necessarily free the asset from memory if the asset's load handle is still held. You must release handles to allow unloading.
Try This
Convert a few transient prefabs to Addressables and compare memory in the Profiler before and after releasing their handles.

screens.title: What Addressables provide
screens.subtitle: Addresses, labels, groups, catalogs, and async APIs

narration.text: Addressables is Unity's managed system that replaces ad-hoc asset loading with a single, unified abstraction. At its heart are addresses and labels: a string address or one or more labels let you reference an asset without a direct scene or inspector link. Addressable Groups are collections of assets that will be packaged into asset bundles by the Addressables build; configuring groups determines packaging, hosting location, and update boundaries. The Content Catalog is the manifest that maps addresses and labels to the physical bundles and their locations. At runtime you interact with the system through asynchronous calls such as Addressables. LoadAssetAsync, which return AsyncOperationHandles you can await or monitor. This creates a clean separation: your gameplay code asks for an address and receives an asset when it's ready, regardless of whether it was loaded from local bundles or downloaded from a remote host. A common confusion is thinking Addressables eliminates the need to manage asset lifetimes. In fact, Addressables gives you the tools to manage lifetimes precisely, but you must call Addressables. Release when you are done to decrement reference counts. Think of Addressables as an orchestration layer that automates bundles and gives you safe, async access to assets.

keyIdea.title: Addressables Overview
keyIdea.text: Addressables abstracts asset bundles into addresses, groups, and catalogs, and exposes async APIs for safe on-demand loading.

content.html:
Definition
What Addressables provide
A unified API to load, host, and update assets by address rather than direct references.
Addresses & Labels
Stable strings or labels that point to assets and support grouping and lookup.
Addressable Groups
Group assets by update cadence or packaging requirements for independent builds.
Content Catalog
A manifest that maps addresses to the physical location of bundles, local or remote.
Async API & Handles
LoadAssetAsync returns an AsyncOperationHandle you await and later release to free memory.
Concrete scenario
Tag character models with a "Characters" label and host that group remotely to update new character packs without a client update.
Common mistake
Assuming Addressables automatically unload unused assets; you must call Release on handles when done.
Key Takeaway

Addressables give you addressable references and catalogs so you can load assets on demand and update them remotely.

screens.title: Install and initialize Addressables
screens.subtitle: Package install, Addressables settings, and the Groups window

narration.text: Getting started is a small number of editor steps that set up the Addressables pipeline. First, install the Addressables package from the Package Manager under the Unity Registry. This adds the Addressables tools and runtime. Next, open Window, Asset Management, Addressables, Groups and initialize Addressables; the system will create settings and a default local group. Initializing is essential because it creates the settings asset that controls build profiles, catalogs, and group rules. After initialization, you can create new groups from the Groups window for characters, environments, UI, or any update domain. A useful pattern is to separate frequently updated content into its own group so you can rebuild and host it remotely independently of stable content. A common misconception is that initialization is optional; without settings you cannot build catalogs or use the Addressables build scripts. Try creating a small group, drag a prefab into it, and then run a Default Build to see the generated bundles and content catalog. This hands-on process makes the underlying packing visible and prepares your project for runtime loading. Install and initialize Addressables means install the package, initialize addressables settings, open groups window, and create groups tailored to your update strategy.. In practical terms, package install, addressables settings, and the groups window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Initialization Steps
keyIdea.text: Install the package, initialize Addressables settings, open Groups window, and create groups tailored to your update strategy.

content.html:
Process Flow
Install & Initialize
  1. Open Package Manager and install Addressables from Unity Registry.
  2. Open Addressables Groups and select "Create Addressables Settings" to initialize.
  3. Create Addressable Groups such as Characters, Materials, UI_Icons.
  4. Drag assets into groups and add labels for bulk operations.
  5. Build & inspect bundles with Build → New Build → Default Build Script.
Why it matters
Initialization produces the settings asset and enables build profiles plus the content catalog needed for runtime resolution of addresses.
Concrete example: After initialization, create a "CharacterPrefabs" group and move two prefabs there to test on-demand loading in Play mode.
Key Takeaway

Initialization is the gateway: without settings, groups, builds, and catalogs you cannot resolve addressable assets at runtime.

screens.title: Make assets Addressable
screens.subtitle: Three ways to mark assets: Inspector checkbox, groups, and labels

narration.text: There are multiple ways to make assets Addressable and each has its use. One method is to select an asset in the Project window and check the Addressable checkbox in the Inspector, which assigns a default address usually equal to the asset path. A second method is to open the Addressables Groups window and drag assets directly into a group; this is useful when creating thematic groups like Characters or Materials. The third is to use labels to tag assets across groups for bulk operations or query-based loading. Labels are powerful when you want to request all assets with a specific tag. For example, tag all environment props with an "Environment" label so the runtime can load only that set when entering a region. A common mistake is leaving the default path addresses for many assets without reviewing them; descriptive addresses make remote updates and catalog tracking easier. Also, remember that making an asset Addressable does not by itself change its lifetime at runtime; you still must load it with Addressables. LoadAssetAsync and later release the returned handle. Practically, try marking a cube and sphere prefab addressable, then add them to a "CharacterPrefabs" group to prepare for the loader script.

keyIdea.title: Ways to Address
keyIdea.text: Use the Inspector checkbox, drag into groups, or assign labels to make assets addressable and ready for packaging and runtime lookup.

content.html:
Process
Three ways to make assets Addressable
Inspector checkbox: Select asset and enable Addressable to give it a default address.
Drag into a Group: Use the Addressables Groups window to drop assets directly into a group for packaging rules.
Labels: Add labels to group assets across groups for query-based loading at runtime.
Example
Make MyCube.prefab and MySphere.prefab addressable and add them to a group named "CharacterPrefabs" to test loading and releasing.
Label pattern
Use labels like "Characters", "Environments", "DLC_Pack_1" to group by purpose rather than folder.
Common pitfall
Relying on default addresses can make remote updates harder to track—use readable addresses for assets you plan to update remotely.
Key Takeaway

Choose a method that matches your workflow: checkbox for quick changes, groups for packaging, labels for bulk operations.

screens.title: Addressable Groups and packaging rules
screens.subtitle: Design groups for update boundaries, hosting, and performance

narration.text: Addressable Groups are the architectural unit that determines how assets are packaged into bundles and where they are hosted. When you create a group you choose rules that affect compression, bundling strategy, and the build path. Groups let you isolate content that changes frequently—put DLC, seasonal items, or levels you will update into separate groups so their bundles can be rebuilt and uploaded without touching stable content. Another common strategy is to separate large streaming textures and audio into their own groups to reduce initial download sizes. Hosting targets come from Build Profiles that specify local or remote paths; groups are built according to the selected profile. A misconception is thinking every asset must belong to a single group forever. You can reorganize groups as your project evolves, but be mindful of address stability and catalog updates. In practice, for the hands-on activity we create "CharacterPrefabs" and "Materials" groups, build the default script, and verify the generated asset bundles and content catalog to confirm the packaging aligns with your update plan. Addressable Groups and packaging rules means use groups to control packaging, compression, and hosting. separate frequently updated content to minimize rebuild scope and hosting costs.. In practical terms, design groups for update boundaries, hosting, and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Group Strategy
keyIdea.text: Use groups to control packaging, compression, and hosting. Separate frequently updated content to minimize rebuild scope and hosting costs.

content.html:
Architecture
Designing Addressable Groups
Groups define bundle boundaries and hosting policies. Choose them based on update frequency and runtime needs.
Stable Content Group
Assets that rarely change, built into local bundles for performance.
DLC / Remote Group
Assets that will be updated remotely; host these bundles on a server.
Streaming Group
Large textures or audio streamed on demand to reduce initial memory usage.
Labels & Queries
Use labels to group across groups for runtime queries and bulk loads.
Practical tip
Separate frequently updated content into its own group to reduce upload and rebuild scope when releasing DLC.
Common oversight
Moving assets between groups can change their addresses or bundle IDs; plan migrations carefully to avoid breaking catalog lookups.
Key Takeaway

Group design is an architectural decision: balance update granularity, hosting cost, and runtime performance when planning groups.

screens.title: Addressables.LoadAssetAsync and AsyncOperationHandle
screens.subtitle: How to request, await, check status, and release a loaded asset

narration.text: Loading assets at runtime uses the asynchronous A P I. The common pattern is to call Addressables. LoadAssetAsync with a generic type and either an address string or an AssetReference. The call returns an AsyncOperationHandle that exposes a Task property you can await or a Completed event you can subscribe to. After awaiting, always check the handle's Status to confirm success before using the Result. When finished with the asset, call Addressables. Release on the handle to decrement the reference count and allow unloading. For prefabs, you often instantiate the Result; instantiation does not transfer ownership of the original asset handle. That means you may keep the prefab handle if you will instantiate more objects later, or release it if you only needed one instance and no further instantiations will occur. A common mistake is releasing a handle while instantiated objects still reference the asset; this can lead to unexpected behavior if the runtime unloads the backing memory. A safe pattern is: load, await, instantiate, and then decide ownership—keep or release—based on whether you need the original asset for future spawns. This pattern gives you predictable memory control.

keyIdea.title: Async Load Pattern
keyIdea.text: Call LoadAssetAsync, await the AsyncOperationHandle, check status, use Result, and call Addressables.Release when appropriate to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
LoadAssetAsync & AsyncOperationHandle
// Pattern: load, await, check, use, release
AsyncOperationHandle<GameObject> handle = Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<GameObject>(address);
await handle.Task;
if (handle.Status == AsyncOperationStatus.Succeeded) {
  GameObject go = Instantiate(handle.Result);
  // decide whether to keep or release handle
}
Addressables.Release(handle);
Concrete example
Load a player prefab by AssetReference, wait for the task, instantiate it at spawn, and release the handle if you won't spawn more players from it.
Misconception
Instantiating a prefab does not remove the need to manage the original asset handle; they are separate lifetimes.
Key Takeaway

Use the AsyncOperationHandle lifecycle to reliably load and release assets; treat instantiated objects and asset handles as independent ownerships.

screens.title: Loader script walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Read and reason the provided AddressableLoader and AddressableSceneLoader scripts

narration.text: Let's walk through the practical loader scripts used in the hands-on exercise. The scripts expose AssetReference fields for prefabs and materials so you can assign Addressables in the Inspector without direct scene references. In Start, the loader calls methods to load the player prefab and a background texture. Each load uses LoadAssetAsync and assigns the returned AsyncOperationHandle to a private field so it can be released later. After awaiting the handle's Task, the code checks AsyncOperationStatus. Succeeded and then uses the Result to instantiate or apply a texture. The example also shows loading by address string for an enemy prefab, awaiting the handle, instantiating, and then immediately releasing that handle. The OnDestroy method demonstrates a defensive release pattern: check if each handle IsValid and call Addressables. Release to ensure memory is freed when the loader is destroyed. Pay attention to the comment about when to keep a prefab handle: if you plan to spawn many instances, keep the handle; if you only need a single instance, release it after instantiation. This walk-through ties the A P I to real project decisions about ownership and lifetime.

keyIdea.title: Loader Pattern
keyIdea.text: Expose AssetReference fields, store AsyncOperationHandles for release, await tasks, check success, and release handles in OnDestroy or when done.

content.html:
Hands-on Example
AddressableSceneLoader pattern
public AssetReferenceGameObject cubeReference;
private AsyncOperationHandle<GameObject> _playerLoadHandle;
async void LoadPlayerPrefabAsync() {
  _playerLoadHandle = Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<GameObject>(cubeReference);
  await _playerLoadHandle.Task;
  if (_playerLoadHandle.Status == AsyncOperationStatus.Succeeded) {
    Instantiate(_playerLoadHandle.Result);
  }
}
void OnDestroy() {
  if (_playerLoadHandle.IsValid()) Addressables.Release(_playerLoadHandle);
}
Concrete guidance
Store handles in fields if you plan to release later. Release immediately if you only need a one-off load.
Common mistake
Not checking IsValid before calling Release can be safe-guarded; always check to avoid runtime errors.
Key Takeaway

The loader script pattern makes ownership explicit: store handles, await success, use results, and release when safe to free memory.

screens.title: Memory management: Addressables vs Resources
screens.subtitle: Why Release matters and how to avoid leaks

narration.text: A practical way to understand Addressables is by contrasting it with the Resources workflow. With Resources. Load, assets are accessible by name but all assets placed in Resources are included in the build, so you cannot avoid build-time bloat. Additionally, Resources. UnloadUnusedAssets is an imprecise tool for freeing memory because it relies on garbage-collector-driven behavior and can leave unexpected references. Addressables gives explicit control: every LoadAssetAsync returns an AsyncOperationHandle and you call Addressables. Release on that handle when the asset is no longer needed. This deterministic release decrements an internal reference count and allows the runtime to unload the backing memory. A typical leak occurs when developers instantiate a prefab from a loaded handle and then destroy the instance but forget to release the loaded handle; Addressables will keep the asset in memory because a handle still indicates interest. To avoid leaks: track your handles, decide whether handles are shared for repeated spawns, and always release in OnDestroy or after a final use. In short, Addressables requires discipline but offers the tools for precise memory control that Resources cannot provide.

keyIdea.title: Memory Contrast
keyIdea.text: Resources is coarse and static; Addressables is explicit and dynamic. Releasing handles is essential to avoid memory retention.

content.html:
Comparison
Addressables vs Resources
Resources: Name-based loading, all assets in Resources included in build, coarse unloading.
Addressables: Address-based loading, groups define packaging, explicit release with handles enables deterministic unloading.
Practical example
Loading a character from Resources cannot be trimmed at build time. Loading via Addressables and releasing allows you to free its memory when it is no longer needed.
Leak scenario
Instantiate a prefab then forget to Addressables.Release the load handle; the asset stays loaded even after destroying the instance.
Best practice
Track handles in a list or fields, release each valid handle once you no longer need the asset or further instantiation.
Key Takeaway

Addressables gives precise control; consistent handle release is the single most important habit to prevent memory leaks.

screens.title: Build Profiles and Content Catalogs
screens.subtitle: How profiles determine hosting and how catalogs map addresses to bundles

narration.text: Build Profiles and Content Catalogs are the operational bridge between your editor and runtime. Build Profiles let you define where bundles and catalogs are written: common profiles are Local Hosted for development and Remote Hosted for production where bundles are uploaded to a web server. When you run a build, Addressables compiles groups into asset bundles and generates a content catalog that lists every address and its associated bundle location. At runtime the Addressables system reads the catalog to resolve an address to a local bundle path or a remote URL. For DLC workflows, you produce a new build for only the groups that changed, upload the new bundles and catalog, and then clients call Addressables. CheckForCatalogUpdates and Addressables. UpdateCatalogs to fetch the new catalog. That catalog points to new bundle locations so the game can download new content on demand. A misconception is expecting the client to automatically discover new content without checking and updating catalogs. Always call the catalog update APIs at an appropriate startup point if you support live content updates. Build Profiles and Content Catalogs means profiles decide build and host targets; the content catalog maps addresses to bundle locations so clients can fetch updated content on demand.. In practical terms, how profiles determine hosting and how catalogs map addresses to bundles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Catalog & Profile Role
keyIdea.text: Profiles decide build and host targets; the content catalog maps addresses to bundle locations so clients can fetch updated content on demand.

content.html:
Build Configuration
Profiles & Catalogs
Profiles determine where bundles are written. Catalogs map addresses to those bundles.
Local Hosted: Useful for development and quick iteration.
Remote Hosted: Upload bundles and catalogs to a server for live updates and DLC.
Catalog updates: Clients must check and apply new catalogs to discover new or changed assets.
DLC flow
Rebuild changed groups, upload bundles and the updated content catalog, then clients update catalogs and load new assets on demand.
Common oversight
Not testing catalog updates can lead to missing assets or mismatched bundle versions on clients; validate update paths early.
Key Takeaway

Use build profiles to control hosting, and treat the content catalog as the single source of truth for resolving addresses at runtime.

screens.title: Dynamic content updates and DLC
screens.subtitle: Check, update, and load new content without a client rebuild

narration.text: Addressables enables dynamic updates and DLC by using remote hosting and the content catalog as the discovery mechanism. The runtime pattern is: at startup or at a safe point, call Addressables. CheckForCatalogUpdates to determine if a newer catalog exists. If updates are available, call Addressables. UpdateCatalogs to download the new catalog and refresh the mapping of addresses to bundle locations. After updating, any subsequent LoadAssetAsync call will resolve through the new catalog and download new bundles as needed. In practice, a team might place new levels and cosmetic packs in an independent group, build and upload that group's bundles and a new catalog, and then let clients fetch the catalog to discover the new content. A common misconception is that you must rebuild the entire game client; with Addressables, only the bundles and catalog need updating server-side. When designing this flow, ensure the client gracefully handles missing bundles, shows progress, and resumes interrupted downloads. This approach allows you to ship new content rapidly without forcing players to update via the store. Dynamic content updates and DLC means check and update the content catalog, then load assets via addresses to fetch new bundles and dlc without a client update.. In practical terms, check, update, and load new content without a client rebuild. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Live Update Flow
keyIdea.text: Check and update the content catalog, then load assets via addresses to fetch new bundles and DLC without a client update.

content.html:
Dynamic Content
Updates & DLC
Use catalog checks to discover new content and download bundles on demand without a full client update.
Step 1: Addressables.CheckForCatalogUpdates to detect new catalogs.
Step 2: Addressables.UpdateCatalogs to download the new catalog.
Step 3: Load assets by address and let Addressables fetch needed bundles.
Host updated bundles separately so you can publish small DLC patches.
Ensure client handles missing bundles with friendly messaging and retry support.
Validate catalog versioning and avoid address renames that break existing references.
Key Takeaway

With catalogs and remote hosting you can push new content and let clients download it on demand, enabling DLC and live updates without client rebuilds.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core terms and practices to recall

narration.text: To retain mastery, remember three core ideas. First, Addressable Assets are assets you reference by address or label for on-demand loading. Second, AsyncOperationHandle is the unit returned by LoadAssetAsync; you must check its status and call Addressables. Release to free memory. Third, Addressable Groups and the Content Catalog determine how assets are packaged and discovered at runtime. Together these ideas let you package content for remote hosting, load only what is needed, and push updates without a full client rebuild. Keep these terms in mind as you migrate prefabs and materials: addresses are stable handles, groups are your packaging policy, and the catalog is the runtime map. Key Concepts means addresses, handles, and groups/catalogs form the operational core of the addressables workflow.. In practical terms, core terms and practices to recall. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memorable Trio
keyIdea.text: Addresses, handles, and groups/catalogs form the operational core of the Addressables workflow.

content.html:

screens.title: Key Concepts — Practical Tips
screens.subtitle: Three actionable reminders for day-to-day work

narration.text: Here are three practical reminders you can apply immediately. First, always store AsyncOperationHandles you will need to release and check IsValid before calling Addressables. Release. Second, use AssetReference fields in scripts to avoid direct scene references and make Inspector-driven loading simpler. Third, plan Addressable Groups around update boundaries so rebuilding is minimal and targeted. Each reminder supports a habit: track handles to avoid leaks, prefer AssetReference for safer assignment, and split groups to enable efficient DLC and remote hosting. These small operational practices repay themselves by preventing common errors and enabling reliable content updates. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Operational Reminders
keyIdea.text: Track handles, prefer AssetReference, and design groups by update cadence to keep builds and runtime behavior predictable.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.6 › Practical Tips
Apply daily
Track Handles
Keep AsyncOperationHandles in fields or lists and release them when finished.
Prefer AssetReference
Expose AssetReference in scripts to assign Addressables in the Inspector without direct references.
Group by Update Cadence
Put frequently updated content in its own group so you can rebuild and host it independently.
Final Takeaway

Small operational habits—tracking handles, using AssetReference, and planning groups—prevent leaks and make updates safe and efficient.

ai_generation_note: Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start with a scene containing a few prefabs and materials. Demonstrate making them Addressable, creating custom Addressable Groups ("Characters", "Environments"), and assigning assets to them. Then, write a script that uses `Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<GameObject>()` to asynchronously load and instantiate a prefab, and `Addressables.LoadAssetAsync<Material>()` to load and apply a material. Crucially, demonstrate calling `Addressables.Release()` to unload assets and show the memory impact in the Unity Profiler. Explain `AssetReference` in the Inspector. Finally, show how to build Addressables content locally and briefly touch upon the concept of remote hosting via Build Profiles. Use a split-screen view of code, Unity Editor, and Addressables Groups window. Include an interactive element where learners predict the memory impact before and after releasing an asset.
